interactions.summary: A student reads the encounter with three noble Florentines, and Jiang emphasizes that even the city's most admired aristocrats share Brunetto's punishment while also naming excess and arrogance as the current disease of Florence.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang explicitly raises the status of the three shades by saying even Virgil respects them.

claims.claim: Jiang says the next canto worsens the paradox because three highly distinguished Florentine aristocrats admired in life are condemned alongside Brunetto.
The read passage identifies the city's new condition as one of excess and arrogance brought by newcomers and quick gains.

signature_moments.moment: Excess and arrogance become the shorthand for Florence's decline.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This compact pair becomes one of Jiang's main tags for mapping Dante's Florence onto modern decline.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture now scales the Brunetto problem up from one beloved teacher to the moral fate of an entire admired elite class.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang again attributes the nobles' presence there to homosexuality in compressed terms; keep that as his framing while preserving the textual scene separately.
